name: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
aliases: low blood glucose in the newborn

clinicalPearls: Low blood glucose is common in the transitional period after birth as the newborn adapts from continuous placental glucose supply to intermittent feeding.
Infants at highest risk include those of diabetic mothers, large- or small-for-gestational-age babies, preterm infants, and any newborn who is stressed, cold, or septic.
Signs are often subtle and non-specific: jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, temperature instability, apnoea, or seizures; many affected infants appear asymptomatic.
At-risk and symptomatic infants should be screened with bedside glucose testing, with low values confirmed on a laboratory sample given the imprecision of point-of-care meters.
Early and frequent feeding is the first-line measure; infants who cannot maintain adequate glucose or who are symptomatic require intravenous dextrose.
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with a documented low glucose that resolves when glucose is normalised (Whipple triad) warrants investigation and treatment.
Persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the first days of life suggests an underlying disorder such as hyperinsulinism, endocrine deficiency, or an inborn error of metabolism.
The clinical concern is that prolonged or severe low glucose can injure the developing brain, so prevention and prompt correction are priorities.
reference.pathophysiology: After the cord is cut, the newborn loses its steady maternal glucose supply and must mobilise hepatic glycogen, activate gluconeogenesis, and use alternative fuels such as ketones and lactate, processes driven by a surge in counter-regulatory hormones and a fall in insulin. When glycogen stores are limited (prematurity, growth restriction), glucose demand is high (stress, sepsis, hypothermia), or insulin secretion is excessive (infant of a diabetic mother, hyperinsulinism), this adaptation fails and blood glucose falls. Because the neonatal brain depends heavily on glucose, inadequate supply combined with immature ketogenesis in some infants places the brain at risk.
additionalInvestigations: Critical sample during hypoglycaemia (insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones, free fatty acids) when persistent
Metabolic screen (ammonia, lactate, acylcarnitine profile) in recurrent or refractory cases
redFlags: Persistent hypoglycaemia despite feeding and initial glucose infusion
High glucose infusion requirement suggesting hyperinsulinism
Recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the transitional period
Associated hypotonia, poor feeding, or encephalopathy
reference.prognosis: Brief, promptly treated transitional hypoglycaemia in an otherwise well infant usually has an excellent outcome, whereas severe, prolonged, symptomatic, or recurrent hypoglycaemia carries a risk of long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.
pitfalls: Treating an isolated low bedside meter reading without confirming on a laboratory sample or clinical context
Assuming all at-risk infants are symptomatic, or dismissing subtle signs as normal newborn behaviour
Failing to investigate hypoglycaemia that persists or recurs beyond the first days of life
Overlooking hyperinsulinism when a high rate of glucose infusion is needed to keep glucose normal
management: Initiate early, frequent feeding (breast or formula) as first-line treatment for at-risk and mildly affected newborns
Escalate to intravenous dextrose for symptomatic hypoglycaemia or when feeding fails to normalise glucose
Investigate and treat persistent hyperinsulinism with diazoxide, reserving octreotide or glucagon for unresponsive cases
Correct and prevent contributing factors such as hypothermia, sepsis and inadequate intake
Confirm low bedside glucose values on a laboratory sample given point-of-care imprecision
Draw a critical (hypoglycaemia) sample during a low-glucose episode in persistent cases and pursue a metabolic and endocrine work-up
Refer refractory or congenital hyperinsulinism to specialist endocrine and metabolic services
